# Relationships Between Teachers' Attitudes, Concerns, Self‐Efficacy, Intentions, and Behavior to Include Students With Disabilities in Regular Schools

# in Cambodia

Sokunrith Pov[1](#relationships-between-teachers-attitudes-concerns-selfefficacy-intentions-and-behavior-to-include-students-with-disabilities-in-regular-schools) \| Norimune Kawai[2](#relationships-between-teachers-attitudes-concerns-selfefficacy-intentions-and-behavior-to-include-students-with-disabilities-in-regular-schools)

1Graduate School of Humanities and Social Sciences, Hiroshima University, Higashihiroshima, Japan \| 2The Institute for Diversity and Inclusion, Hiroshima University, Higashihiroshima, Japan

Correspondence: Sokunrith Pov ([sokunrithp@gmail.com)](mailto:sokunrithp@gmail.com) Received: 10 June 2024 \| Revised: 29 November 2024 \| Accepted: 14 February 2025

Keywords: attitude \| behavior \| behavioral intention \| concern \| inclusive education \| self‐efficacy \| theory of planned behavior

ABSTRACT In Cambodia, students with disabilities remain marginalized and excluded from regular education settings, leading to low attendance and primary education completion rates. These challenges highlight critical concerns about teachers' inclusive practices. This study utilized the Theory of Planned Behavior to explore how teachers' attitudes (attitudes toward inclusion), subjective norms (concerns about inclusion), perceived behavioral control (self‐efficacy for inclusive prac- tices), and behavioral intentions shaped their actual behavior to include students with disabilities. A survey was con- ducted with 1008 in‐service teachers from 236 primary schools across Cambodia using the teachers' attitudes toward inclusion scale, concern about inclusive education scale, and teacher efficacy for inclusive practices. Data analysis employed a mediation analysis using structural equation modeling with the lavaan package in RStudio. The study revealed that subjective norms and perceived behavioral control significantly and directly predicted teachers' intentions to support students with disabilities. Behavioral intentions, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control also directly predicted their actual behavior. Indirect effects showed that subjective norms and perceived behavioral control significantly predicted actual behavior through behavioral intentions. The findings highlight the importance of strengthening policy and training programs to alleviate teachers' concerns and enhance their self‐efficacy to promote inclusive practices.

Summary

- This study provides theoretical and empirical insights into the relationships between Cambodian teachers' at- titudes, subjective norms (concerns about inclusion), perceived behavioral control (self‐efficacy for inclusive practices), behavioral intentions, and their actual behavior toward inclusion, laying a strong foundation for effective policy and practice improvements to en- hance teachers' behavior in including and supporting students with disabilities.
- The study found that for direct effects, teachers' sub- jective norms and perceived behavioral control signifi- cantly predicted their behavioral intentions to support inclusion. Subjective norms, perceived behavioral con- trol, and behavioral intentions significantly predicted actual behavior toward inclusion. For indirect effects, subjective norms and perceived behavioral control sig- nificantly predicted the actual behavior through behav- ioral intentions.
- The study advocates for policy reforms in Cambodia, emphasizing systematic policy dissemination with on‐ site support, compulsory inclusive education training, curriculum modification skills, aligned training dura- tion, extended training efforts, an improved training model, shared responsibility, collaborative support, school leadership involvement, better resource access, and further research on the effectiveness and challenges of inclusive education courses and field experiences.

Cambodia has demonstrated strong commitments to SDG4, making it a key priority in its Education Strategic Plans 2019–2023 and 2024–2028. The Ministry of Education, Youth and Sport (MoEYS) prioritizes education policy “en- suring all Cambodians have access to quality, equitable, and inclusive education enriched with knowledge, skills, disci- pline, ethics, good behavior, health, fitness, and lifelong learning” (MoEYS 2019b, 2024). This commitment not only facilitates the expansion of educational projects and the establishment of systems to support students with SEND, particularly students with disabilities (SWDs), but also holds the potential for significant positive change in the Cambodian education system. Notable initiatives include the establishment of special education schools, the National Institute of Special Education (NISE), and the Department of Special Education to advance both special and inclusive education for SWDs (Pov 2021).

Legislation further supports these efforts. Article 39 of Cam- bodia's Law on Education affirms the right of SWDs to be educated alongside peers without disabilities in regular class- rooms through curriculum modifications rather than separate curricula (Cambodia National Assembly [2007)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-). To further address the needs of SWDs, MoEYS introduced the Policy on Education for Children with Disabilities in 2008 (see MoEYS 2008). After 10 years of its implementation, this policy was revised into the Policy on Inclusive Education in 2018 (see MoEYS 2018). The Policy on Inclusive Education builds on the previous policy and aims to further integrate SWDs into regular schools, providing additional support and resources for teach- ers. These policies reinforce this right and encourage teachers to

2238 of 2338

accept SWDs into regular education classrooms (Cook and Cameron [2010)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-).

Data from the Education Management Information System (EMIS) for the academic year 2021–2022 classify disabilities into four categories: physical, intellectual, mental, and other dis- abilities. Physical disabilities, including movement, visual, and hearing impairments, are the most prevalent, particularly at the primary level, followed by intellectual disabilities, as shown in Figure 1. Mental disabilities and other conditions are the least reported across educational levels (MoEYS 2023). The defini- tions of these terms are detailed in the “Determination of Criteria for Types and Levels of Disabilities” (see Ministry of Social Affairs, Veterans, and Youth Rehabilitation. 2011). These statistics reflect a growing number of SWDs in regular schools, presenting substantial challenges in achieving a fully inclusive education system (Disability Action Council [2003)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-).

In regular school settings, while some schools admit students with low‐incidence disabilities, only a few accommodate a broad range of conditions and varying severity levels, including hearing, visual, and intellectual impairments (Kalyanpur [2016;](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-) Ravet and Mtika 2021). In Cambodia, SWDs face significant challenges in accessing the curriculum due to the lack of nec- essary modifications to address their specific needs. Often, they are placed in so‐called “inclusive classes” without receiving the additional tailored support from teachers (Nishio 2019).

2 \| Framing the Problems

Despite various government's commitments, a significant number of children with disabilities remain out of school, while SWDs are marginalized within regular classrooms and continue to drop out before completing an educational cycle, especially at the primary level. According to the UNESCO Institute for Sta- tistics (2018), 57% of Cambodian children with disabilities of primary school age (6–11 years old) were out of school, com- pared to only 7% of their peers without disabilities. Further- more, only 44.4% of SWDs completed primary education, with the remaining 55.6% dropping out of schools. Similarly, the 2019 population census reported that 44.3% of individuals aged seven and over with disabilities completed primary education (UNESCO Institute for Statistics 2018).

The needs of SWDs extend beyond mere school attendance. They require tailored support and assistance from teachers to participate fully in regular classrooms (Disability Action Council [2003)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-). Achieving the principle of inclusion necessitates changes to values, attitudes, policies, and, most importantly, teachers' practices (Polat 2011). Teachers play a crucial role in implementing inclusive practices, determining the success or failure of inclusive education (Forlin and Lian [2008)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-). They translate inclusive education policies into changes in teaching practices, making it imperative to address their attitudes, con- cerns, self‐efficacy, intentions, and behavior toward inclusion (Emmers et al. [2020;](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-) Shah et al. 2016; Yan and Sin 2014).

While previous studies have commonly investigated teach- ers' attitudes and self‐efficacy, and the factors influencing them (e.g., Agbenyega [2007;](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-)Alnahdi[2019;](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-)Ekins et al.[2016;](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-)

4 \| Theoretical Framework

Understanding individuals' behavior in all its complexity is challenging. Ajzen ([1991)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-) asserts that to comprehend an in- dividual's behavior,

It can be approached at many levels, from concern with physiological processes at one extreme to concentration on social institutions at the other. Social and personality psychologists have tended to focus on an intermediate level, the fully functioning individual whose processing of available information mediates the effects of biological and environmental factors on behavior.

(p. 179)

The Theory of Planned Behavior provides a robust theoretical framework for understanding how teachers' behavior is shaped within regular education settings. This study serves as a guiding framework to examine whether Cambodian in‐service teachers' attitudes toward behavior regarding attitudes toward inclusion, subjective norms regarding concerns about inclusion, and per- ceived behavioral control regarding self‐efficacy for inclusive practices, and behavioral intentions significantly predicted their actual behavior toward acceptance or rejection of SWDs in their classrooms. In principle, the theory posits that individuals' behavioral intentions are influenced by their attitudes toward the behavior, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control. Behavioral intentions and perceived behavioral control, in turn, shape their actual behavior to perform an action (Ajzen [1991)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-).

Ajzen ([1991,](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-) 188) defines attitude toward behavior as “the degree to which a person has a favorable or unfavorable evaluation or appraisal of the behavior in question.” Subjective norms involve “the perceived social pressure to perform or not to perform the behavior.” Perceived behavioral control refers to “the perceived ease or difficulty of performing the behavior, and it is assumed to reflect past experience as well as anticipated impediments and obstacles.” In essence, more positive attitudes and subjective norms, along with stronger perceived behavioral control, lead to greater behavioral intentions to perform a par- ticular behavior. The significance of attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control varies across behaviors and situations (Ajzen [1991)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-). These aspects are particularly crucial in the field of inclusive education to examine their significant association with teachers' behavior in implementing inclusive practices (Emmers et al. [2020;](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-) Urton et al. 2023; Yan and Sin 2014).

In the context of inclusive education, the Theory of Planned Behavior is a robust theoretical framework commonly used to explain attitudes, concerns, and self‐efficacy in implementing inclusive practices that shape in‐service teachers' behavioral intentions and actual behavior in including SWDs in regular classrooms. Attitudes toward behavior are conceptualized as individuals' perceptions, such as their attitudes toward

2240 of 2338

inclusion, regarding the characteristics and outcomes of including SWD in regular classrooms, evaluated based on their assessments of these aspects. Subjective norms pertain to teachers' perceptions of the views of significant others (e.g., colleagues, students without disabilities, and parents) on inclusive education, considering their motivation to adhere to these beliefs. Perceived behavioral control involves teachers' perceptions of their ability to implement inclusive practices, particularly self‐efficacy for inclusive practices, concerning their knowledge of strategies and their sense of control over the implementation process (Scanlon et al. 2022; Yadav et al. 2015).

5 \| Previous Studies

Research shows that the Theory of Planned Behavior has been employed as a framework in several studies to examine how teachers' attitudes, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, and behavioral intentions influence their actual behavior in implementing inclusive practices (e.g., Emmers et al. [2020;](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-) Urton et al. 2023; Yan and Sin 2014). This theory is particularly relevant in studies exploring in‐service teachers' actual behavior and its determinants, especially in terms of the inclusion or rejection of SWDs in regular classrooms.

In Flanders, Emmers et al. ([2020)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-) utilized the Theory of Planned Behavior to examine the relationships between atti- tudes, self‐efficacy, and behavior toward inclusion of teachers from all higher education institutions. The study employed the Teacher Efficacy for Inclusive Practices (TEIP), developed by Sharma et al. (2012), and the Sentiments, Attitudes, Con- cerns regarding Inclusive Education‐Revised (SACIE‐R) scales, developed by Forlin et al. ([2011)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-). Attitudes toward behavior were measured using SACIE‐R, specifically the attitude scale assessing attitudes toward inclusion. Subjective norms were assessed using three items that gauged teachers' beliefs about how important individuals in the learning en- vironment talked about SWDs. Perceived behavioral control was assessed using the 18‐item TEIP. Behavioral intentions were measured with a four‐item scale related to how teachers label SWDs, while actual behavior was assessed using a three‐ item scale focusing on communication with SWDs. The study found that only attitudes had a significant impact on behav- ioral intentions, while subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, and behavioral intentions did not significantly influence actual behavior.

In Germany, Urton et al. (2023) utilized the Theory of Planned Behavior to measure factors explaining primary school teachers' intentions to implement inclusive practices. In their study, at- titudes were divided into behavioral beliefs and outcome ex- pectations, measured by three key aspects: academic learning, social development, and social inclusion for students with and without special educational needs. Subjective norms were divided into normative beliefs and motivation to comply, mea- sured by the beliefs of the ministry, the school inspectorate, the school principal, colleagues, parents, and students. Perceived behavioral control was divided into control beliefs and per- ceived power, measured by three aspects: cooperation, resources, and knowledge. The study found that all these factors

Psychology in the Schools, 2025

had significant relationships with teachers' behavioral inten- tions to implement inclusion.

In Hong Kong, Yan and Sin (2014) used the Theory of Planned Behavior to analyze predictors explaining teachers' behavioral intentions and behavior toward inclusion. The study involved 841 primary and secondary school teachers from regular schools. The study found that attitudes toward behavior, sub- jective norms, and perceived behavioral control had a signifi- cant influence on behavioral intentions to implement inclusive practices. Furthermore, intentions, along with attitudes toward behavior, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control, significantly influenced actual behavior toward inclusion. Similarly, a recent study by Yang et al. (2024) confirmed that attitudes toward behavior, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control significantly impacted both behavioral intentions and behavior. Additionally, the study revealed that intentions and behavior significantly mediated the effects on the social and academic competencies of students with special educational needs in Hong Kong.

These studies collectively underscore the importance of un- derstanding the relationships between attitudes toward behav- ior, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, behavioral intentions, and behavior toward inclusion, using the Theory of Planned Behavior as a guiding framework. The relationships among these factors differ across samples and the country‐ specific contexts. It would be intriguing to explore these re- lationships among Cambodian teachers, considering the varia- tions in school and resource contexts for implementing inclusive education.

To date, no studies have examined these relationships among Cambodian in‐service teachers, nor have any studies employed theoretical frameworks with large samples for generalization purposes. Some studies have focused on teachers' attitudes and the implementation of training programs related to inclusive education (e.g., Nishio 2019; Kuroda et al. 2017; Pov et al. 2024; Ravet and Mtika 2021). The present study seeks to fill these gaps, offering implications for improving policies and practices to enhance teachers' behavior toward the inclusion of SWDs, with the ultimate goal of improving enrollment rates and reducing dropout rates among SWDs in regular education settings.

6 \| Methodology

6.1 \| Study Design

This study employed a quantitative approach using a correla- tional research design for the investigation. In essence, corre- lational research serves two primary purposes to elucidate significant human behaviors through naturalistic observation by (1) exploring relationships among variables, and (2) to pre- dict likely outcomes of one variable in relation to other variables that are not manipulated during the research period (Fraenkel et al. [2011;](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-) Privitera 2016). This study design aligns with the study's objective of predicting the likely outcomes of teachers' actual behavior toward inclusion based on their attitudes to- ward behavior, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control,

and behavioral intentions. Furthermore, the design supports the study's goal of generalizing findings to all primary school teachers in Cambodia.

6.2 \| Participants

The selection of schools for this study was based on a cluster random sampling method, considering school location (urban and rural areas) and the school's track record in accommodat- ing SWDs. A list of all primary schools in Cambodia in the academic year 2021–2022 was obtained from EMIS of MoEYS. Primary schools were filtered based on location and the inclu- sion of SWDs, resulting in 1314 eligible schools. From this pool, primary schools were randomly selected from each province, resulting in 236 primary schools across 25 provinces and cities in Cambodia. All teachers from the selected schools were invited to participate in the current study, with a total of 1008 teachers voluntarily completing the questionnaire, with a response rate of 71%. Detailed participant characteristics are presented in the “Results” section.

6.3 \| Instruments and Variables

This study employed a four‐part questionnaire for data collec- tion, comprising (1) demographic background, (2) the 24‐item Teachers' Attitudes Toward Inclusion Scale (TATIS), (3) the 18‐item TEIP scale, and (4) the 21‐item Concerns about Inclu- sion Scale (CIES).

Attitudes toward behavior were measured using the TATIS scale, which was originally developed by Bailey ([2004)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-). This 24‐item scale, rated on a 5‐point Likert scale (1 = strongly dis- agree, 2 = disagree, 3 = neither disagree nor agree, 4 = agree, and 5 = strongly agree), comprises five subscales: (1) imple- mentation issues, (2) benefits of inclusion, (3) learning chal- lenges, (4) exclusion of SWDs, and (5) professional training. Implementation issues address challenges regarding fairness, practicality, and the impact of inclusion on workload, class time, and other students' learning. Benefits of inclusion capture perceived academic and social advantages of inclusion. Learn- ing challenges reflect difficulties in accommodating SWDs due to their specific needs. Exclusion of SWDs emphasizes beliefs about excluding students with behavioral challenges. Profes- sional training highlights concerns over inadequate teacher preparation (see Bailey [2004)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-).

Subjective norms were measured using the 21‐item CIES, which was originally developed by Sharma and Desai (2002). Rated on a four‐point scale (1 = not concerned at all, 2 = a little con- cerned, 3 = very concerned, 4 = extremely concerned), the scale includes four subscales: (1) resources, (2) workloads, (3) aca- demic standards, and (4) acceptance. Resources address con- cerns about insufficient funding, staff, infrastructure, and support. Workloads highlight concerns about increased work- load, lack of incentives, and staff stress. Academic standards reflect concerns about declining academic standards, teacher performance, and student attention. Acceptance indicates con- cerns about time to plan for SWDs, maintaining discipline, and

2241 of 2338

lack of knowledge and skills to teach them (see Sharma and Desai 2002).

Perceived behavioral control was measured using the TEIP scale, which was originally developed by Sharma et al. (2012). It consists of 18 items, rated on a six‐point scale (1 = strongly disagree; 2 = disagree; 3 = disagree somewhat; 4 = agree some- what; 5 = agree; 6 = strongly agree). The scale includes three subscales: (1) managing behaviors, (2) collaboration, and (3) using inclusive instruction. Using inclusive instruction high- lights confidence in assessment, alternative explanations, task design, and student engagement. Managing behavior reflects confidence in handling disruptions, enforcing rules, and managing aggression. Collaboration captures confidence in supporting families, working with professionals, involving parents, and educating others on inclusion policies (see Sharma et al. 2012).

Behavioral intentions were evaluated by teachers' intentions to support SWDs in regular classrooms. Previous studies also used several items to determine teachers' behavioral intentions, fo- cusing on their willingness to support SWDs (see Urton et al. 2023; Yan and Sin 2014). In the analytical model, behav- ioral intentions served as a mediator between attitudes, sub- jective norms, and perceived behavioral control.

Teachers' actual behavior toward inclusion served as the outcome variable, assessed based on their real‐life experi- ences of accepting or rejecting SWDs throughout their teaching careers. This approach has been utilized in previ- ous studies (e.g., Cook and Cameron [2010)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-). Actual behavior toward inclusion was a dichotomous dependent variable (0 = not included SWDs, 1 = included SWDs). Teachers were asked to report their experiences of including or rejecting SWDs in their classrooms.

As described in the sampling procedure, this study included 50% of schools with inclusive education programs. Despite this, only 45% of teachers reported having experience ac- cepting SWDs into their classrooms, while 55% reported rejecting them. This finding raises serious concerns about the underlying attitudes, concerns, and self‐efficacy that may contribute to such negative behavior (see Emmers et al. [2020;](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-) Kroesch and Peeples [2021;](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-)Urton et al.2023;Yan and Sin 2014).

6.4 \| Data Collection and Ethical Issues

To collect data, ethical approval and permission were obtained from Hiroshima University and MoEYS. In Japan, ethical approval was granted by the Research Ethics Review Board of Hiroshima University (reference #HR‐ES‐000805) in Japan on 24 February 2023. In Cambodia, permission for data collection was granted by MoEYS (reference #735) on 6 February 2023. Permission was also secured from the target schools, and individual consent was obtained from the participants to address ethical considerations. Conse- quently, the questionnaire was distributed to all teachers in 236 primary schools, resulting in 1008 valid responses, with a 71% response rate.

6.5 \| Data Analysis

Descriptive statistics, including mean (M), standard deviation (SD), and frequency, were used to calculate the attitude, con- cern, self‐efficacy, intentions, behavior, and demographic characteristics of the participants. For the validity test, an Ex- ploratory Factor Analysis using Principal Axis Factoring (PAF) with Equamax rotation was employed to explore the underlying structure of the 24‐item TATIS, 21‐item CIES, and 18‐item TEIP using data from Cambodian teachers. Subsequentially, reli- ability tests (Cronbach's Alpha) were conducted to assess the internal consistency and reliability of the general scales and subscales of these instruments.

The mediation analysis using structural equation modeling (SEM) with the lavaan package in RStudio (version 2024.09.0 + 375) was utilized to examine the direct, indirect, and total effects of teachers' attitudes toward behavior, subjec- tive norms, perceived behavioral control, and behavioral intentions on their actual behavior toward inclusion. This model was based on Ajzen's ([1991)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-) Theory of Planned Behavior (see Figure 2). Three primary variables were included as pre- dictors: attitudes (AT), subjective norms (SN), and perceived behavioral control (PBC), along with one mediator, behavioral intentions (BHI). The binary outcome variable was behavior toward inclusion (BH).

Given the categorical nature of the outcome variable (0 = not included SWDs, 1 = included SWDs), the robust diagonally weighted least squares (DWLS) estimator was employed to address non‐normality data distribution. DWLS is particularly suited for binary and ordinal outcome variables, as it provides robust standard errors and chi‐square test statistics, making it an appropriate choice for this analysis (Mîndrilă. 2010).

To assess the effects of the mediation, a bootstrapping proce- dure with 5000 resamples was utilized to estimate the Confi- dence Interval (CI) for the indirect effects. Bootstrapping is a non‐parametric resampling method that allows for more accu- rate CI estimation without relying on the assumption of nor- mality in the sampling distribution of the indirect effects. This method yields robust estimates for mediation analysis by com- puting bias‐corrected bootstrap CI for indirect effects. The sta- tistical significance of the indirect effect was assessed using the bootstrap CI method. If the 95% CI for the indirect effect does not include zero, the mediation effect is deemed statistically significant (see Hayes [2022)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-).

To ensure that the model fitted with the data, various fit indexes were considered as prerequisites for interpreting the estimated results. The chi‐square test (χ2) indicates whether there is a significant difference between the model‐implied covariance matrix and the original covariance matrix (Fan et al. [2016)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-). This test should yield a nonsignificant result (p \> 0.05) (Hu and Bentler [1999)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-). The values of the comparative fit index (CFI) and Tucker–Lewis index (TLI) should meet the threshold value of

0.90 (Hu and Bentler [1999;](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-) Kline [1998,](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-) [2023)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-). The root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) should have a cut‐off value close to 0.08, and the standardized root mean square residual (SRMR) should be below 0.09 to indicate a good model fit (Hu and Bentler [1999)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-).

FIGURE 2 \| Mediation model.

As a prerequisite step before estimating a mediation model, Pearson correlation was computed to examine the strength and direction of the linear relationships between all variables included in the model. Subsequently, the analysis assessed the direct, indirect, and total effects of attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control on actual behavior toward inclusion, with intentions as a mediator. Figure 2 presents the direct and indirect paths, as well as the covariances between the three predictors: attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control.

For direct paths, the model estimated whether attitudes toward behavior (a2 =AT → BHI), subjective norms (a1 =SN → BHI), and perceived behavioral control (a = PBC → BHI) significantly predicted behavioral intentions (BHI). Subsequently, it esti- mated whether these predictors, together with behavioral intentions, significantly predicted behavior (BH) toward the inclusion of SWDs.

For indirect paths, the model examined whether attitudes to- ward behavior (a2b =AT → BHI → BH), subjective norms (a1b =SN→ BHI → BH), and perceived behavior control (ab = PBC → BHI → BH) significantly predicted actual behavior through behavioral intentions (BH), with behavioral intentions (BHI) acting as the mediator.

7 \| Results

7.1 \| Participants' Characteristics

Table 1 presents the participants' characteristics. Among the participants, 33% were male and 67% were female. Regarding their educational background, 12% had an education level below a diploma, 58% held a diploma, 1% had an associate degree, 28% possessed a bachelor's degree, and 1% held a master's degree. In terms of teaching experience, 27% had 1 to 5 years of experience, 22% had 6 to 10 years, 15% had 11 to 15 years, and 36% had 16 years or more. Approximately 71% of the teachers worked in rural schools, with the remaining 29% in urban schools. In this study, 45% of the teachers had experience accepting SWDs into their classrooms, while 55% had experi- ence rejecting them.

7.2 \| Validity and Reliability of the Instruments

For the validity test, the Exploratory Factor Analysis using PAF with Equamax rotation was used to examine the factor structure of the instruments (TATIS, CIES, andTEIP) using Cambodian teacher samples. For the attitude scale (TATIS), the PAF model unveiled a total of five factors that explain 43% of the total variance, aligning with Bailey ([2004)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-). The Kaiser‐Meyer‐Olkin (KMO) measure con- firmed the sample's adequacy (KMO = 0.80). Bartlett's test of sphericity was statistically significant (χ2 (190) = 5516.66, p \< 0.001), showing that the variables' correlations were sufficient for the model. The alpha coefficients (α) were 0.75 for the benefits of inclusion, 0.73 for learning challenges, 0.72 for implementation is- sues, 0.85 for the exclusion of SWDs, 0.76 for professional training, and 0.74 for the general attitude scale.

For the self‐efficacy scale (TEIP), the PAF model unveiled a total of three factors that account for 56.77% of the total variance, aligning with Sharma et al. (2012). The KMO measure indicated the ade- quacy of sampling for the analysis (KMO = 0.94). Bartlett's test of sphericity was statistically significant (χ2 (136) = 9676.72, p \< 0.001), suggesting that the variables' correlations were sufficient for the model. The alpha coefficients (α) were 0.91 for managing behaviors,

0.87 for collaboration, 0.81 for using inclusive instruction, and 0.93 for the general self‐efficacy scale.

For the concern scale (CIES), the PAF model unveiled a total of four factors that account for 57.26% of the total variance, aligning with Sharma and Desai (2002). The KMO measure indicated the ade- quacy of sampling for the analysis (KMO = 0.93). Bartlett's test of sphericity was statistically significant (χ2 (120) = 8109.09, p \< 0.001), indicating that the variables' correlations were sufficient for the model. The alpha coefficients (α) were 0.84 for resources, 0.86 for workloads, 0.85 for academic standards, 0.72 for acceptance, and

0.91 for general concern scale.

7.3 \| Correlation Coefficients

Table 2 indicates that attitudes toward behavior had significant relationships with subjective norms (r = −0.38, p \< 0.01), per- ceived behavioral control (r = 0.09, p \< 0.01), behavioral inten- tions (r = 0.13, p \< 0.01), and the actual behavior toward

Subjective norms had significant but negative relationships with perceived behavioral control (r = −0.16, p \< 0.01), behavioral intentions (r = −0.19, p \< 0.01) and the actual behavior (r = −0.15, p \< 0.01). Additionally, perceived behavioral control had significant and positive correlations with both behavioral intentions (r = 0.25, p \< 0.01) and the actual behavior (r = 0.16, p \< 0.01). Lastly, behavioral intentions had a significant and positive relationship with actual behavior toward the acceptance or rejection of SWDs (r = 0.27, p \< 0.01). These results indicated weak correlations.

7.5 \| Covariance Estimates

Table 4 presents the results of the covariance estimation between the three predictors: attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control. The covariance between attitudes and subjective norms was statistically significant (β = −0.38, SE = 0.01, p \< 0.001). The covariance between attitudes and perceived behavioral control was also statistically significant (β = 0.09, SE = 0.01, p \< 0.01),

Lastly, the covariance between subjective norms and perceived behavioral control was statis- tically significant (β = −0.16, SE = 0.01, p \< 0.001). This nega- tive association suggests that higher subjective norms are associated with lower perceived behavioral control.

8 \| Discussion

8.1 \| Effects on Teachers' Behavior Toward Inclusion

Using the Theory of Planned Behavior as a theoretical frame- work, this study found that for direct effects, subjective norms and perceived behavioral control significantly predicted behavioral intentions to support the inclusion of SWDs. Fur- thermore, behavioral intentions and perceived behavioral con- trol, in turn, significantly predicted actual behavior. In terms of indirect effects, subjective norms and perceived behavioral control significantly predicted actual behavior through behav- ioral intentions. These findings indicate that teachers with higher levels of self‐efficacy for inclusive practices, more posi- tive behavioral intentions to support inclusion, and lower levels of concerns about inclusion demonstrated significantly more positive behaviors in including SWDs in their classrooms compared to their counterparts.

Similarly, Urton et al. (2023) employed the Theory of Planned Behavior to assess how attitudes, subjective norms, and per- ceived behavioral control influenced primary school teachers' intentions to implement inclusive practices in Germany. The study found that subjective norms regarding normative beliefs and motivation to comply significantly influenced teachers' intentions. Among these, normative beliefs at the administra- tive level had the strongest impact on intentions. Moreover, perceived behavioral control regarding cooperation, resource availability, and knowledge positively influenced teachers' intentions. Notably, control beliefs related to collaboration and expertise in special education had the greatest effect on teach- ers' intentions to implement inclusive education.

Yan and Sin (2014)utilized Ajzen's ([1991)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-) theoretical framework to identify key predictors of teachers' behavior in implementing inclusive practices in Hong Kong and found that teachers perceived significant social pressure to adopt inclusive practices, whereas they indicated positive perceived behavioral control, strong intentions, and active engagement in inclusion. Notably, concerns about social pressure directly influenced behavioral intentions and indirectly negatively impacted actual behavior through these intentions.

Perceived behavioral control, particularly confidence gained from professional training, also had significant direct and indirect effects on actual behavior through intentions (Yan and Sin 2014). Simi- larly, a recent study by Yang et al. (2024) supported that subjective norms and perceived behavioral control significantly impacted both behavioral intentions and actual behavior. These aspects also sig- nificantly influenced the social and academic competencies of stu- dents with special educational needs in Hong Kong.

Urton et al. (2023), Yan and Sin (2014), and Yang et al. (2024) concurred that among all predictors, perceived behavioral control, particularly in terms of self‐efficacy for inclusive prac- tices, was the strongest predictor influencing in‐service teach- ers' intentions and actual behavior toward the inclusion of SWDs in primary and secondary school classrooms. These findings underscore the need to move beyond cultivating posi- tive attitudes and theoretical understanding of inclusive edu- cation. While teachers may express positive attitudes toward inclusion, they often indicate significant concerns regarding inadequate training and the need for more effective support to teach SWDs (Ravet and Mtika 2021). Addressing these concerns extends beyond mere school attendance. It calls for substantial changes in teaching practices (Disability Action Council [2003)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-). Practical guidance is essential for teachers to effectively inte- grate inclusive education principles into their teaching, tailored to their unique classroom contexts (Woodcock et al. 2022).

The findings of previous studies align with those of the current study, emphasizing that teachers' self‐efficacy emerges as the most influential predictor of both their behavioral intentions and behavior toward inclusion. These findings underscore the pressing need to enhance teachers' sense of self‐efficacy and address their concerns to effectively implement inclusive practices. Such improvements can be achieved by enhancing policy support, teacher preparation programs for pre‐service teachers, and ongoing training programs for in‐service teachers. These programs should focus on equipping teachers with practical skills and knowledge regarding inclusive practices (Ekins et al. [2016;](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-)Emmers et al.[2020;](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-) Pijl 2010;Pov et al.2024;Urton et al.2023;Yan and Sin2014). However, these areas have been identified as significant challenges to the effective implementation of inclusive practices in Cambodia (Kuroda et al. 2017; Ravet and Mtika 2021). To improve teachers' inclusive practices, thisstudy suggestssome implications for im- proving policy and practices.

8.2 \| Implications for Policy and Practice

In Cambodia, the policies and action plans for inclusive edu- cation lack robust implementation, stimulate specialized

Psychology in the Schools, 2025

curricula, and enforce conditional inclusion for students with SEND (UNICEF 2020). To alleviate teachers' concerns and foster their positive attitudes, self‐efficacy, and behavior toward the inclusion of SWDs, it is imperative to prioritize policy re- forms that eliminate specialized curricula and conditional inclusion, while integrating local understandings of disability (Kalyanpur [2016;](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-) Pov and Kawai 2024). The reforms should facilitate systematic policy dissemination at the school level, accompanied by on‐site support. This approach will ensure that education practitioners, especially teachers, gain a compre- hensive understanding of inclusive education (King [2018;](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-) Kuroda et al. 2017) and adjust their values, attitudes, and practices to better support students with SEND (Polat 2011).

This process may involve re‐evaluating the existing cascade training model (King [2018)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-) and incorporating on‐site support for teachers, school principals, and school administrators to offer practical guidance on translating policies into practices (Kuroda et al. 2017). For instance, on‐site support involves guiding teachers, school principals, and school administrators to revise school policies, including vision and mission state- ments, and develop action plans for school improvement that align with the Policy on Inclusive Education (see MoEYS 2018) and Action Plan on Inclusive Education (see MoEYS 2019a). These initiatives can significantly influence teachers' attitudes, self‐efficacy, and concerns, and assist them in collaboratively developing accommodation and modification strategies to sup- port SWDs alongside their peers without disabilities.

Research indicates that most in‐service teachers in Cambodia have not received adequate inclusive education training. Even those who have undergone training often find it insufficient and ineffective to prepare them for inclusive classroom settings (Kuroda et al. 2017; Pov and Kawai 2024; Ravet and Mtika 2021). Similarly, pre‐service teachers face numerous challenges in preparing for inclusive classrooms, stemming from various deficiencies in teacher education programs. Despite some exposure to inclusive education courses in both old and newly reformed teacher education programs, pre‐ service teachers often lack the necessary practical knowledge, skills, and experience to implement inclusive practices effec- tively (Pov et al. 2024). These deficiencies have significant impacts on teachers' attitudes, concerns, and self‐efficacy in implementing inclusive practices, not only in Cambodia (e.g., Kuroda et al. 2017; Pov et al. 2024; Ravet and Mtika 2021) but also in other countries (e.g., Alnahdi [2019;](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-) Costello and Boyle [2013;](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-) Forlin et al. [2011;](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-) Sharma and Sokal 2015).

To address teachers' concerns about inclusion and enhance their self‐efficacy and behavior toward inclusive practices, several implications for both pre‐service and in‐service training programs need to be considered. Despite positive attitudes toward inclusion, Cambodian in‐service teachers express significant concerns about their ability to effectively implement inclusive practices, particularly due to a lack of resources in rural schools (Ravet and Mtika 2021). Training efforts should specifically target teachers in inclusive edu- cation settings, especially those in rural areas with limited support and resources. Revisiting the current cascade train- ing model and integrating on‐site support and hands‐on ex- perience will ensure that teachers develop practical skills

alongside theoretical knowledge (King [2018;](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-)Kuroda et al. 2017).

Training programs for in‐service teachers should focus on developing the skills necessary for implementing curriculum modifications. Integrating modified curricula into general education classrooms has been shown to significantly improve students' academic outcomes, reduce disruptive behaviors, and, importantly, enhance teachers' sense of self‐efficacy in mana- ging student behavior and classroom activities (Lee et al. 2010). Moreover, fostering a sense of shared responsibility among teachers, promoting collaborative support for inclusive prac- tices, involving school leadership teams in the inclusive edu- cation process, and providing access to resources are all crucial steps in creating and fostering an inclusive culture and advancing inclusive practices at the school level (Emmers et al. [2020;](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-) Pijl 2010; Valdés and Gómez‐Hurtado 2023).

For pr‐eservice teachers, the current training programs at the primary and lower secondary levels allocate only 6 h to inclu- sive education, which is far less than the 28 h and 25 min required to complete the newly developed inclusive education training guidebook. This guidebook consists of 19 modules (see MoEYS 2017). This misalignment limits pre‐service teachers' access to comprehensive inclusive education training. Further- more, it is essential to integrate inclusive education courses as mandatory components of pre‐service teacher training pro- grams, rather than treating them as “optional additions” to the curriculum. By ensuring full access to inclusive education courses, pre‐service teachers will gain the confidence and acquire the skills needed to include SWDs in their future classrooms (Ekins et al. [2016;](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-) Pov et al. 2024). Additionally, given the limited research on pre‐service and novice teachers' inclusive practices, there is a need for more comprehensive studies to explore the effectiveness and challenges of inclusive education courses and field experiences for both pre‐service and in‐service teachers (Kroesch and Peeples [2021)](#10--limitations-and-future-studies-disability-action-council-2003-inclusive-education-training-in-cam-).

9 \| Conclusion

The Theory of Planned Behavior emerges as a robust frame- work for understanding in‐service teachers' behavior toward inclusion and the factors influencing these behaviors in Cam- bodia. The findings align with previous research, indicating that Cambodian in‐service teachers' concerns about inclusion and self‐efficacy for inclusive significantly influenced their actual behavior toward the inclusion of SWDs in regular classrooms. This study underscores the pressing need for policy reforms, advocating for systematic policy dissemination at the school level with on‐site support for teachers. It emphasizes the importance of integrating compulsory inclusive education training into pre‐service programs, ensuring the alignment with the newly developed inclusive education guide. In addition, the study calls for extending training efforts for in‐service teachers and revising the existing cascade training model to integrate on‐ site support and hands‐on experience, enabling teachers to develop practical skills alongside theoretical knowledge. Training programs should prioritize equipping teachers with the skills needed to implement curriculum modifications effectively. Moreover, fostering a sense of shared responsibility
